Charlemagne. Around 748 to 814, he was king of the Franks and crowned emperor of the Romans. He unified much of Western Europe and laid the foundation for the later kingdoms of France and Germany. His reign marked a cultural renaissance and the re-establishment of centralized authority after Rome's collapse.

On Christmas Day in the year 800, Pope Leo III crowned him Emperor of the Romans. It was the first such coronation since the fall of the Western Roman Empire, and Charlemagne's empire stretched from the Pyrenees to the Danube, claiming a restored Roman dominion. To secure his vast territory, he conquered and subdued Saxony through brutal campaigns, expanding Frankish lands and Christianizing the pagan peoples of Northern Europe.

But Charlemagne was more than a warrior. He established the Carolingian Renaissance, sponsoring scholars and monasteries. He standardized Latin script, what came to be called Carolingian minuscule, which preserved classical texts that might otherwise have been lost. He convened councils at his palace in Aachen, creating centers of learning and reforming the clergy and ecclesiastical structure across his realm.

He had inherited a fragmented kingdom from his father Pepin III, and he transformed it into the largest Western European empire since ancient Rome. Yet his empire fractured remarkably quickly. Within a generation, the Treaty of Verdun in 843 partitioned it into what would become France, Germany, and Italy, dividing his grand vision among his heirs.
